newsitem.title: USA: FBI explores possibility of Atlanta serial bomber.
newsitem.headline: FBI explores possibility of Atlanta serial bomber.

text.p: The FBI said on Saturday a serial bomber could be at work after the fourth bomb to strike Atlanta in seven months exploded at a popular gay nightclub on Friday night, injuring five people.

The bomb, apparently packed with nails, went off in the rear patio section of the Otherside Lounge in northeast Atlanta shortly before 10 p.m. EST. Staff said the club, frequented mostly by lesbians, was about half full at the time.
Police found a second bomb in a backpack hidden among some bushes near an adjacent parking lot, and detonated the device with a remote-control robot.
Both police and nightclub staff said there was no prior warning of an attack.

Investigators from the FBI and the U.S. Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms said the attack bore similarities to two previous incidents in Atlanta -- a January double-bombing at an abortion clinic and the deadly Centennial Olympic Park bombing last July.

"We all recognise that there are similarities here. We will be searching out the possibility that we have a serial bomber," Woody Johnson, the special agent in charge of the Atlanta FBI office, told a news conference early on Saturday.
There was no hard evidence linking the nightclub bombing to the earlier attacks.

Of the five people hurt, only one was taken to hospital. She was identified as Memrie Wells-Crestwell of Snellville, Ga. A spokesman for Grady Memorial Hospital said the woman underwent surgery to remove shrapnel from her right shoulder on Saturday morning and was later listed in stable condition.
Gay rights activists condemned the bombing as a hate crime reminiscent of Ku Klux Klan attacks on black civil rights activists in the South in the 1960s.
"Maybe this was something to scare us, to put us in our place," local gay activist Lynn Cothren told a television interviewer.

"But we intend on continuing our struggle and continuing to have places of business that we own, that we patronise, and not to live in fear and intimidation. We will not let this bomb, or any other kind of hate, send us back into the closet," he said.

The first emergency call from the nightclub said a man and a woman had been shot. Members of the city's SWAT team were the first to arrive at the scene and quickly spotted the backpack that contained the second bomb.
Police, later joined by the FBI and ATF, sealed off several blocks around the club while agents walked the empty roadways after sunrise in search of bomb shrapnel and other debris.
Nightclub patrons reported seeing a flash, followed by a blast they said resembled an exploding electrical transformer.
The woman who was initially believed to have been shot rolled up her sleeve to find a three- to four-inch (8-10 cm) nail sticking through her arm, according to eyewitnesses.
"I can't believe it," nightclub owner Beverly McMahon said. "We just don't have problems and this is incredible."
"We clearly believe that we are dealing with a deranged killer, but one that is very clever as well," Atlanta Mayor Bill Campbell said.

Police investigators said Friday's bombing was similar to a double-bomb attack on an Atlanta abortion clinic in January that injured half a dozen people, mostly law enforcement agents and rescue workers.
As in that attack, the second device at the nightclub was placed in an apparent attempt to injure police and rescue workers responding to the initial emergency call.

The use of a backpack for the second device resembled the Centennial Olympic Park bombing in July. In that incident, a pipe bomb packed with nails and hidden in a green military-style knapsack exploded during a crowded outdoor concert in downtown Atlanta, leaving two people dead and more than 100 wounded.
Both the abortion-clinic bombing and the Centennial Olympic Park bombing remain unsolved.
